opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it: if you look at what models can do today, on short tasks they're already superhuman in a lot of ways. Give a model a well-scoped problem, a math question, a function to write, an essay to draft, and it will often do better and faster than most experts. Raw intelligence over a few minutes of work isn't really the bottleneck anymore.

What breaks down is when you ask the system to work on something for hours, days, or weeks, in an open-ended domain where there isn't a clean verifier. Real work looks like that. You have a goal that's somewhat fuzzy, you take thousands of actions, you hit dead ends, you have to notice you made a mistake three steps ago and recover, you have to keep track of what you've learned, and you have to know when you're actually done. Each individual step might be 99% reliable, but compound that over a thousand steps and you basically never finish correctly. So reliability, not capability, is the binding constraint.

And it has to be general-domain. We've seen that if you can build a good reward signal for a narrow domain, like coding with unit tests or competition math, you can push long-horizon performance quite far with RL. But most valuable work doesn't come with a unit test. Making a business decision, running a research project, managing someone's finances: the feedback is delayed, noisy, sometimes subjective. Getting models to be robustly reliable there, without hand-building an environment for every task, is the hard part.

Why I'd call it probably the last big one is that if you solve it, the rest mostly follows. A system that can reliably pursue an arbitrary goal over long horizons can do research, including AI research, can learn new skills on the job, can correct itself. At that point you've effectively got something that can do most knowledge work end to end. Other open problems, like continual learning, memory, or efficiency, either become sub-problems of long-horizon reliability or get easier once you have it. So it's not that everything else is trivial, but this is the piece that stands between very impressive assistants and systems that can actually be trusted to go do the job.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's the last big one because almost everything else we point at turns out to be a special case of it. If you look at where models fail today, it's rarely that they can't do a step. They can do the step. They fail when you chain a thousand steps together across a day or a week of work, in a domain where nobody wrote a clean reward function for you. Each step has some small probability of a mistake, and over a long enough horizon those compound into near-certain failure. That's the thing that stands between "impressive demo" and "I'd actually hand this my job."

The reason it's hard is that the two words in that phrase pull against each other. Long-horizon reliability in a narrow domain is tractable. Games showed us that. Coding is showing us that, because you get verifiable signal, tests pass or they don't. Where there's a verifier, you can do reinforcement learning, you can search, you can grind the error rate down. The problem is that most of the world isn't like that. Most valuable work has fuzzy success criteria, depends on context the model has to go find rather than being handed, and the mistakes are quiet. Nobody tells you at step forty that step twelve was wrong. So "general-domain" means you lose the verifier, and "long-horizon" means you can't afford even small error rates. Solve either alone and you don't get the thing people actually want.

And I'd argue if you solve both, there's very little left. Reasoning, tool use, memory, planning, self-correction, knowing when to ask for help, those aren't separate problems anymore. They're the ingredients you need in order to be reliable over a long horizon in an open domain. So I don't think of it as one problem on a list. I think of it as the problem the list collapses into. Once a system can take an ambiguous, multi-week goal and come back with the right answer at the rate a good human colleague does, most of what we'd call AGI is already there. Everything after that is scaling and economics, not research.

astra-6.text:
Because there’s a big difference between being able to do a difficult thing once and being able to reliably execute a whole project. A model can give you a brilliant answer, write a useful piece of code, or solve a hard problem, and still make enough small mistakes that you can’t leave it working independently for a week.

And those mistakes compound. If each step has a high probability of success, but you need thousands of steps, the probability that everything goes right can still be very low. Of course, humans make mistakes too. The important capability is noticing that you made one, understanding what went wrong, and recovering before you build another hundred steps on top of it.

The general-domain part makes this especially hard. In a narrow setting, you can often build a verifier or put guardrails around the system. But if the task involves writing code, talking to people, interpreting ambiguous requirements, and changing the plan as new information comes in, there isn’t one simple signal that tells you whether you’re on track.

So I think the remaining gap is increasingly between intelligence that you can access in short bursts and intelligence that you can actually delegate to. Once a system can take a broad goal and reliably pursue it over long periods, checking its own work and asking for help when appropriate, that unlocks a very large fraction of the practical value we want from AI.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we’ve gotten very good at making models that can solve a hard problem in isolation. But that’s different from having a system you can give a broad goal to and trust to work on it for hours or days, across all the different situations it encounters.

If you’re doing a long task, you make thousands of decisions. A small mistake early on can change what you see next, and then you’re reasoning from a false assumption. So it’s not just about getting each individual step right. You need to notice when something went wrong, check your work, recover, and sometimes reconsider the whole approach.

In a narrow domain, you can build a lot of that structure around the model. You can have a clear success criterion, a verifier, a constrained environment. In the general case, the system has to figure out what to verify and what success even looks like. Sometimes it needs to ask you a question; sometimes it should keep going.

That’s why I think reliability is such a big remaining problem. We already have a lot of the capabilities you’d want in individual moments. The challenge is making them hold together over a long stretch of work, including when the system encounters something unexpected.
